summary: Fed minutes point to more rate hikes, Lowe's and Palo Alto raise their outlooks, Alibaba's cloud growth speeds up, and a Lyft experiment shows a premium option can push buyers toward the cheapest one.

news.title: Fed minutes show almost all officials expect further rate hikes, and a couple raised the idea of a half-point move
news.tldr: Minutes of the Fed's October 27-28 meeting show officials held rates at 3.75-4% but almost all expect more hikes, setting up a December debate over how fast to tighten.
news.why_selected: Central-bank guidance on the path of US interest rates, which sets borrowing costs across the economy.

sections.heading: Context
sections.body: The US Federal Reserve raised its policy rate in September and then paused at its October 27-28 meeting, keeping the federal funds rate, the overnight rate banks charge each other, in a range of 3.75% to 4%. Inflation has been running above 3% a year, well above the Fed's 2% target. The minutes of each meeting are published three weeks later and show how officials argued behind closed doors.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.body: The minutes, released Wednesday at 2 p.m., show that "almost all" officials agreed further rate hikes would be needed if the economy evolved as they expected, according to the Globe and Mail. A few said inflation could prove more persistent, and "a couple" argued the Fed might need a half-percentage-point increase if inflation data were unfavourable. The vote to hold was 10 to 2: Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack wanted a quarter-point (25 basis point) hike. Fed staff estimated that inflation by the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) measure rose to 3.6% in September, with core PCE, which excludes energy and many food prices, at 3.1%. A few officials called the decision to hold "a close call."

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.body: The minutes confirm that the Fed is debating how much and how fast to tighten, not whether to stop. Staff attributed higher inflation to earlier tariffs, energy prices and price pressure linked to the AI investment boom, and noted that debt tied to the AI buildout was growing rapidly. Officials also stressed that pausing did not weaken their commitment to 2% inflation. Higher policy rates feed through to mortgages, car loans and corporate borrowing, and the staff projected inflation of about 2% only in 2028. Market pricing cited in the minutes put high odds on a 25 basis point hike by year-end.

sections.heading: What to watch
sections.body: The Fed meets again on December 8-9. The Globe and Mail reports investors expect a quarter-point increase; a larger move or tougher guidance is the open question.

news.title: Lowe's raises its full-year sales forecast to about $92.5 billion as online sales jump 17.4%
news.tldr: Lowe's comparable sales rose 1.8% last quarter and it now expects full-year sales of about $92.5 billion, though it trimmed its margin forecast as costs rise.
news.why_selected: Results from a bellwether for US spending on homes and home improvement.

sections.heading: Context
sections.body: Lowe's is a Fortune 100 home-improvement retailer with more than 1,750 stores and about 300,000 employees. Its sales track how much Americans spend on their homes, which has been held back by a weak housing market. Over the past year it bought Foundation Building Materials (FBM) and Artisan Design Group (ADG) to grow its business with professional contractors.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.body: On November 18, Lowe's reported net earnings of $1.7 billion, or $2.98 a share, for the quarter ended October 30, up from $2.88 a year earlier. Adjusted earnings per share rose 1.3% to $3.10. Total sales grew to $22.8 billion from $20.8 billion, and comparable sales, which strip out new and closed stores, rose 1.8%, helped by a 17.4% increase in online sales and solid sales to professionals and of home services. Earnings included about $250 million, or $0.34 a share, from refunds of IEEPA tariffs. Lowe's raised its full-year sales forecast to about $92.5 billion from $92 billion and now expects comparable sales to rise about 0.5% instead of staying flat.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.body: This was Lowe's sixth quarter in a row of positive comparable sales, CEO Marvin Ellison said, which suggests home spending is holding up even in a slow housing market. But much of the headline sales growth came from acquisitions, and the company cut its operating margin forecast to about 11.1% from 11.2%, citing cost pressures. The one-off tariff refund also flattered this quarter's profit. For suppliers and contractors, the shift toward professional customers and online orders shows where the growth is.

sections.heading: What to watch
sections.body: Lowe's will set out its growth plans at an analyst and investor conference in December.

news.title: Palo Alto Networks raises its revenue forecast after 39% growth and agrees to buy Applied Compute for $4.5 billion in stock
news.tldr: The cybersecurity company now expects fiscal 2027 revenue of up to $14.57 billion and is buying an AI model-training startup founded only last year.
news.why_selected: A guidance raise and a multibillion-dollar deal at a bellwether for corporate security spending.

sections.heading: Context
sections.body: Palo Alto Networks is a cybersecurity company. It has been growing by acquisition, completing purchases of Chronosphere and CyberArk early in 2026, and is trying to show investors that companies will keep spending on security as they adopt AI systems.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.body: After the market closed on November 18, Palo Alto reported revenue of $3.44 billion for its fiscal first quarter ended October 31, up 39% from a year earlier and above the $3.31 billion analysts expected, Proactive Investors reported. Adjusted earnings were $1.05 a share. Annual recurring revenue from its Next-Generation Security subscriptions rose 66% to $9.73 billion. The company raised its fiscal 2027 revenue forecast to $14.52-14.57 billion from $14.10-14.20 billion. It also announced an all-stock deal valued at $4.5 billion for Applied Compute, a startup founded in 2025 by three former OpenAI researchers that helps businesses train and run their own AI models. The shares rose about 9% to 11% in after-hours trading.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.body: The raise suggests corporate security budgets are holding up; the finance chief cited "the current threat environment and demand." But MLQ.ai notes the release does not say how much growth came from acquisitions, since the year-ago quarter predates the CyberArk and Chronosphere deals, and GAAP operating income fell to $96 million from $309 million as stock-based pay and amortization rose. Paying in stock means existing shareholders are diluted rather than the company taking on debt. Applied Compute raised money earlier this month at a $3.25 billion valuation.

sections.heading: What to watch
sections.body: The Applied Compute deal needs regulatory clearance and is expected to close in Palo Alto's fiscal third quarter.

news.title: Alibaba's cloud revenue grows 53% as AI demand accelerates, but heavy spending keeps free cash flow negative
news.tldr: Alibaba's group revenue rose 10% to about $40.5 billion, its AI cloud unit grew 53%, and free cash flow was an outflow of $5.1 billion as data-centre spending climbed.
news.why_selected: Results from a major Chinese e-commerce and cloud group, a gauge of Chinese consumer demand and AI investment.

sections.heading: Context
sections.body: Alibaba runs online marketplaces in China and a fast-growing cloud computing business. Investors have been weighing fast growth in its AI cloud unit against the cost of building data centres and losses in quick commerce, its rapid-delivery service. Its shares had fallen 42% since the start of 2026, Grafa reported.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.body: Alibaba said on Thursday that revenue for the quarter ended September 30 rose 10% from a year earlier to 271.5 billion yuan (about $40.5 billion). Revenue from AI Cloud and Compute Services rose 53% to about $9.1 billion, accelerating from 45% growth in the June quarter, and recurring revenue from outside customers grew 67%. AI-related product revenue grew at a triple-digit rate for the 13th quarter in a row. Adjusted EBITA, a profit measure that excludes some non-cash items, rose 260% as losses in quick commerce narrowed. Free cash flow, the cash left after capital spending, was an outflow of 34.5 billion yuan (about $5.1 billion), and capital spending rose 60%. Shares were down 2.6% in premarket trading.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.body: The results show that demand for AI computing in China is translating into revenue, with outside companies building Alibaba's tools into ongoing operations rather than only experimenting. Cloud profitability improved, with the unit's EBITA margin reaching 14.5%. But customer management revenue, which Alibaba earns from merchants on its marketplaces, fell 5%, and Crypto Briefing reports that adjusted earnings per share missed some analysts' estimates. The cash outflow shows how expensive the AI race is, even for a company of Alibaba's size.

sections.heading: What to watch
sections.body: Finance chief Toby Xu said Alibaba is targeting positive free cash flow; whether capital spending slows will be the test.

sources.name: Alibaba Group (Business Wire via Yahoo Finance)

papers.title: Irregular Demand: The Anti-Compromise Effect in the Field
affiliations: Bocconi University; University of Chicago; Australian National University; Washington University in St. Louis
papers.tldr: In a Lyft experiment with 7.2 million riders, adding an expensive premium ride pushed customers toward the cheapest option and toward not riding at all.
papers.why_selected: A very large field experiment that challenges a standard assumption behind product-line and pricing decisions.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.body: Firms constantly add premium tiers: basic and premium economy seats, flagship phones, faster pickups in ride-hailing apps. Standard economic theory says a new product can only draw demand away from existing options; it cannot make any existing option more popular. The authors test whether that "regularity" holds in a real market.

sections.heading: Existing approaches
sections.body: Most evidence on violations of this rule comes from laboratory experiments, where people may behave differently than in real purchases they make repeatedly. Well-known lab findings such as the compromise and decoy effects suggest a premium product should push buyers toward more expensive mid-range options. Two earlier field experiments found either a compromise effect or no effect.

sections.heading: Key idea
sections.body: Working with Lyft between November 2020 and January 2021, the researchers randomly assigned 7,242,942 riders, across 47.6 million app sessions, to a control menu of "Wait & Save" and "Standard" rides, or to the same menu plus a faster, pricier "Fast Pass." They also randomized the Fast Pass price at three levels. Riders did not know they were in a study. John List was Lyft's chief economist when the research was done.

sections.heading: Results
sections.body: Adding Fast Pass lowered demand for Standard, as expected, but raised demand for the cheapest option and the share of riders who requested no ride. In the first session, Wait & Save demand rose by 0.2 to 0.3 percentage points under the medium and high prices, and the effect across all sessions was roughly five times larger. The effect on not buying equalled a 1.17% rise in every Lyft price. It grew with the Fast Pass price and with repeated exposure, and persisted even when Fast Pass was not shown.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.body: Product managers and pricing teams usually assume a premium tier moves customers up the menu; here it moved them down, apparently by making riders pay more attention to price. The authors explain it through memory and salience. The main caveat: this is one platform and one product category, and the paper has not been peer-reviewed.
